First, let's recall the double-angle formula for sine: 

$$
\sin{2x} = 2\sin{x}\cos{x}
$$

Substituting $x=25^\circ$ into the above, we get

$$
\sin\left(2\cdot 25^\circ\right) = 2\sin 25^\circ \cos 25^\circ
$$

which simplifies to

$$
\sin 50^\circ = 2\sin 25^\circ \cos 25^\circ.
$$

Therefore, we can simplify the given expression by rewriting the ${\color{blue} \sin 50^\circ}$ in the denominator as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡{25}^{∘}}{\operatorname{sin}⁡{50}^{∘}} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡{25}^{∘}}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡{25}^{∘}\operatorname{cos}⁡{25}^{∘}} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡{25}^{∘}}}{2\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡{25}^{∘}}\operatorname{cos}⁡{25}^{∘}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡{25}^{∘}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡{25}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's recall the double-angle formula for sine: 

$$
\operatorname{sin}2x=2\operatorname{sin}x\operatorname{cos}x
$$

Substituting $x={40}^{∘}$ into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}(2\cdot {40}^{∘}) & =2\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘} \\ \operatorname{sin}({80}^{∘}) & =2\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can rewrite the given expression using the above, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}{80}^{∘}\operatorname{tan}{40}^{∘}-1}{\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}+\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}} & =\frac{2\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}}{\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}}-1}{\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}+\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}} \\  & =\frac{2{sin}^{2}{40}^{∘}-1}{\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}+\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}} \\  & =\frac{{sin}^{2}{40}^{∘}-1+{sin}^{2}{40}^{∘}}{\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}+\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}} \\  & =\frac{{sin}^{2}{40}^{∘}-(1-{sin}^{2}{40}^{∘})}{\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}+\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}}\end{aligned}
$$

Using  the Pythagorean identity in the form ${cos}^{2}{40}^{∘}=1-{sin}^{2}{40}^{∘},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{sin}^{2}{40}^{∘}-(1-{sin}^{2}{40}^{∘})}{\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}+\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}} & =\frac{{sin}^{2}{40}^{∘}-{cos}^{2}{40}^{∘}}{\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}+\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}} \\  & =\frac{(\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}+\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘})(\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}-\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘})}{\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}+\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}+\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘})}(\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}-\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘})}{\cancel{\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}+\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}}} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}{40}^{∘}-\operatorname{cos}{40}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's recall the double-angle formula for sine: 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡2x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Substituting $x={50}^{∘}$ into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot {50}^{∘}) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡{50}^{∘}\operatorname{cos}⁡{50}^{∘} \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡({100}^{∘}) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡{50}^{∘}\operatorname{cos}⁡{50}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can rewrite the given expression using the above, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡{100}^{∘}\operatorname{tan}⁡{50}^{∘}}{2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡{50}^{∘}} & =\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡{50}^{∘}\operatorname{cos}⁡{50}^{∘}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡{50}^{∘}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡{50}^{∘}}}{2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡{50}^{∘}} \\  & =\frac{2{\sin }^{2}⁡{50}^{∘}}{2(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡{50}^{∘})} \\  & =\frac{{\sin }^{2}⁡{50}^{∘}}{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡{50}^{∘}}\end{aligned}
$$

Using  the Pythagorean identity ${\sin }^{2}⁡{50}^{∘}=1-{\cos }^{2}⁡{50}^{∘},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\sin }^{2}⁡{50}^{∘}}{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡{50}^{∘}} & =\frac{1-{\cos }^{2}⁡{50}^{∘}}{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡{50}^{∘}} \\  & =\frac{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡{50}^{∘})(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡{50}^{∘})}{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡{50}^{∘}} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡{50}^{∘})}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡{50}^{∘})}{\cancel{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡{50}^{∘}}} \\  & =1+\operatorname{cos}⁡{50}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

\frac{2sc}{2c} &=s \\ &=\sin\left(46^\circ\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

All cancellations use nonzero factors in the original expression.

Write $s=\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{14}\right)$ and $c=\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{14}\right)$. The **double-angle formula** gives $\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{7}\right)=2sc$.



Expand the doubled sine and cancel the common factor.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{2sc}{2s} &=c \\ &=\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{14}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

All cancellations use nonzero factors in the original expression.

Write $s=\sin\left(59^\circ\right)$ and $c=\cos\left(59^\circ\right)$. The **double-angle formula** gives $\sin\left(118^\circ\right)=2sc$.

 Also, $\tan\left(59^\circ\right)=\frac{s}{c}$.

Rewrite the quotient ratio and use $s^2+c^2=1$ to obtain a difference of squares. Factor before cancelling.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{2sc\frac{s}{c}-1}{s-c} &=\frac{2s^2-1}{s-c} \\ &=\frac{s^2-c^2}{s-c} \\ &=\frac{(s-c)(s+c)}{s-c} \\ &=s+c \\ &=\sin\left(59^\circ\right)+\cos\left(59^\circ\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

All cancellations use nonzero factors in the original expression.

Write $s=\sin\left(36^\circ\right)$ and $c=\cos\left(36^\circ\right)$. The **double-angle formula** gives $\sin\left(72^\circ\right)=2sc$.

 Also, $\tan\left(36^\circ\right)=\frac{s}{c}$.

Rewrite the quotient ratio and cancel. Use $s^2+c^2=1$, factor the difference of squares, then cancel the matching binomial.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{2sc\frac{s}{c}}{2(1+c)} &=\frac{2s^2}{2(1+c)} \\ &=\frac{1-c^2}{(1+c)} \\ &=\frac{(1-c)(1+c)}{(1+c)} \\ &=(1-c) \\ &=\left(1-\cos\left(36^\circ\right)\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

All cancellations use nonzero factors in the original expression.
